newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Metal-Zinc to shine, metal piles up in S'pore.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metal-Zinc to shine, metal piles up in S'pore.

text.p: Zinc is likely to rise to a fresh 4-1/2 year peak on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Friday as shrinking world stocks stoke fresh fund buying, dealers said.
"Everything looks very, very positive for zinc. The metal should continue rising on followthrough buying," a dealer for a European metal trading company told Reuters.
LME brokers Brandies said in its daily review that zinc closed well on the LME on Thursday despite some profit-taking.
"As a result, the market should go on to test $1,350 in the short term," Brandeis said.

"Everything has become so strong. It's surprising," said Vinod Kumar, director of Singapore metal company Donald Mcarthy. But another dealer said zinc may be overbought and should retrace some of its gains.
"It should come back down on pure profit-taking," he said.
Zinc prices soared to a 4-1/2 year high on Thursday on the London Metal Exchange (LME), closing $43 up on the day at US$1,330 a tonne.
Three-month zinc was seen by Asian dealers at 0400 GMT at $1,328/32 a tonne.

Chinese zinc exporters may try to take advantage and ship some zinc to Singapore, but warehouses in the city-state are jammed with the metal and the Chinese may find it more prudent to sell directly to users in the region, traders said.
The volume of zinc on warrant with the LME's Singapore warehouse reached 12,100 tonnes on Thursday.

"I think there are 25,000 tonnes of zinc not on warrant with the LME warehouse. There's maybe more," a dealer for a European metal dealing house said. "There's a lot of zinc in this part of the world."
One dealer said rumours were circulating in the market that China would ship 5,000 to 10,000 tonnes of zinc to Singapore.
"I doubt the zinc is coming. There's so much here already. They may just want to try and sell it directly to neighbouring countries like Japan, Korea, Taiwan or Indonesia," he said.
But another dealer said any glut in the region was temporary as increasing demand in the second half of 1997 wwould draw down stocks further.
"The fundamental picture for zinc looks bright," he said.

The base metal market in the region was quiet with aluminium demand slow ahead of the negotiations for third quarter supply contracts in Japan, Taiwan and South Korea that are due to begin by mid-May.
"I think demand is going to pick up again after the talks are over," one dealer said.
"I still see quite a lot of spot buying for aluminium," another trader said.
Traders said copper prices may consolidate briefly around $2,400 a tonne before steaming ahead to higher levels over the next few weeks.
"Copper is looking good. It will eventually go to $2,500 (a tonne)," a dealer said.
Copper premiums remained firm, mainly because of drawdowns in the LME's Singapore warehouse. The volume of copper here reached 14,250 tonnes on Thursday, down from a peak of 55,000 tonnes in March.
